posts.title: The Christmas Truce Still Has Something to Teach Us About Leadership and Humanity
posts.linkedin:
The Christmas Truce of 1914 is often reduced to a comforting story about soldiers singing carols, exchanging gifts and playing football. The history is more complicated—and more useful. The truces were local and unofficial, fighting continued elsewhere, and senior commanders discouraged fraternisation. Yet in some places soldiers still chose, briefly, to recognise the humanity of people they had been trained to treat only as enemies.

That is the part I find most relevant to leadership. Leadership does not begin only with authority, policy or title. It also appears in small choices made inside rigid systems: whether to listen, whether to de-escalate, whether to preserve dignity, and whether to recognise another person before treating them as a category. The truce did not end the war, and goodwill did not remove the structures driving the conflict. But it showed that human judgement can still matter even when institutions are powerful.

For organisations, public institutions and enterprises, the lesson is not that conflict can be wished away. It is that systems work better when people retain the capacity for judgement, trust and dignity instead of allowing process or hierarchy to eliminate them.

Full article: https://www.waithakandegwa.com/my-thoughts/christmas-truce-humanity-leadership

posts.title: From Reception Desk to Partnership: What Tong Wenhong’s Alibaba Story Really Teaches
posts.linkedin:
Tong Wenhong’s Alibaba story is usually told as a viral wealth anecdote: a receptionist receives shares, waits patiently, and eventually becomes very wealthy. That version is memorable, but it misses the more important organisational lesson.

Tong joined Alibaba early, moved through several operational and management roles and became part of the company’s long-term leadership story. The useful question is not whether every employee should expect a similar financial outcome. It is whether an organisation can recognise capability early, create room for people to grow beyond their first job description, and design incentives that allow employees to share in value they help create.

For African enterprises, this matters. We often focus heavily on recruiting senior talent from outside while underinvesting in internal mobility, management development and long-term ownership. A receptionist, technician, field officer or junior administrator may understand the organisation in ways that become strategically valuable later. The challenge is to create systems that notice that potential rather than freezing people in the role in which they entered.

Long-term value is strongest when growth in the enterprise can also create growth in responsibility, capability and—where appropriate—shared economic participation for the people who helped build it.

posts.title: Kenya Is Visa-Free — But Travel Is Not Paperwork-Free
posts.linkedin:
Kenya’s move toward visa-free travel is important, but the traveller’s experience is what ultimately determines whether the policy feels open. Visa-free does not mean paperwork-free. Depending on nationality and current exemptions, travellers may still need an Electronic Travel Authorisation, supporting documents, fees or other pre-travel steps.

That distinction matters because policy communication shapes confidence. If a country markets itself as easy to enter but the actual process feels unclear, repetitive or unpredictable, the gap between the promise and the journey becomes part of the visitor experience. The same principle applies beyond immigration: digital public services should be judged not only by what a policy intends, but by how easily a real person can complete the process.

Kenya has made significant progress in opening travel and simplifying entry for many visitors. The next step should be continuous refinement: clearer eligibility rules, fewer unnecessary steps, transparent fees, reliable processing, and communication that matches the actual process people encounter. Openness is not just a policy statement; it is a service design challenge.

posts.title: DHL’s Original Insight Still Matters: Remove Friction Before You Move More Goods
posts.linkedin:
DHL’s early insight was surprisingly simple: move shipping documents ahead of the cargo so customs work can begin before the goods arrive. The company did not start by moving more freight. It started by removing a delay around the freight.

That is a useful way to think about infrastructure in Africa. Roads, ports, railways, airports and warehouses matter, but physical assets alone do not guarantee efficient movement. Documentation, customs processes, information systems, scheduling, coordination, payment, standards and handoffs between institutions can create as much friction as the absence of infrastructure itself.

For entrepreneurs, this creates a practical opportunity. Some of the most valuable businesses do not necessarily build the biggest asset; they make an existing system work better. They reduce waiting time, uncertainty, duplication or coordination costs. In agriculture, construction, trade and manufacturing, a process improvement can sometimes unlock value faster than another large capital project.

The lesson I take from DHL is to look for the friction around the transaction. Before asking how to move more goods, ask what is preventing the goods already moving from moving reliably.

Full article: https://www.waithakandegwa.com/my-thoughts/dhl-friction-logistics-lesson

posts.title: Sugar Beet Could Complement Kenya’s Sugarcane — But It Is Not Yet the Answer
posts.linkedin:
Sugar beet is worth testing in Kenya, but it should not be promoted as a national solution before the agronomy, processing and economics are proven. Kenya still has a significant sugar-supply challenge, and current international data continues to record commercial sugar production as cane-based rather than beet-based.

The trade context also matters. Kenya operated under a COMESA sugar safeguard for more than two decades, using quota-based regional access while the domestic industry was expected to restructure. The final safeguard extension expired on 30 November 2025. On 4 November 2026, President William Ruto publicly said Kenya was now off the COMESA safeguard list, linking that position to debt write-offs, mill restructuring, new factory licences and improved domestic production. The important distinction is that the legal safeguard had already expired; the President’s statement was an industrial-policy declaration that Kenya considers the protection era finished.

That makes competitiveness more important, not less. Kenya still has to manage domestic production, consumer prices, regional trade obligations and periodic deficits. Sugar beet could become one diversification pathway in suitable highland zones, but only if specific varieties produce enough recoverable sugar and if processing, logistics, contracts and offtake are commercially viable.

My preferred approach is therefore a bounded commercial pilot: agronomic trials, multi-season demonstration plots, independent sugar-content measurement, processing feasibility, farmer-contract design and only then wider expansion. Farmers should not be recruited at scale before the factory and market economics are proven.

Full article: https://www.waithakandegwa.com/my-thoughts/sugar-beet-kenya-complement-not-cure

posts.title: Kenya’s Tomato Problem Is Not Just Overproduction — It Is a Processing and Coordination Gap
posts.linkedin:
When tomato prices collapse, the easiest explanation is usually that too many farmers planted at the same time. That is part of the problem, but it is not the whole problem. Kenya’s deeper challenge is that production, processing and market coordination are still poorly connected. KALRO has reported that less than 2% of locally produced tomatoes enter processing, despite the country having a significant number of processors.

That means farmers are largely selling a highly perishable crop into the fresh market. When harvests peak together, the market cannot absorb the volume quickly enough, traders gain bargaining power, losses rise and prices can fall below production cost. Government policy matters—roads, standards, irrigation, market information and competition all affect outcomes—but planting decisions and value-chain organisation also matter.

The more durable solution is not simply to tell farmers to produce more or to blame one actor after every price crash. Production should increasingly be organised around demand: processors, institutional buyers, retailers, hospitality, exporters and other offtakers. Cooperatives or producer organisations can help aggregate volume, negotiate contracts, coordinate planting windows and support quality standards, but only if they are run transparently and commercially.

The opportunity is to build a tomato value chain where farmers know the intended market before planting, processors can rely on consistent supply, and surplus production can move into products with a longer shelf life instead of becoming waste.

posts.title: From Impact Evidence to Economic Demand: What This Week’s Signals Mean for African Social Entrepreneurs
posts.linkedin:
Social entrepreneurship is getting better at measuring impact. The harder question is what happens after the measurement: who will actually pay for, procure, invest in or otherwise support the outcomes we can prove?

Current signals point in the same direction. The World Economic Forum and Schwab Foundation are arguing that impact disclosure has to become connected to real economic demand. Social Finance has announced new impact-first investments in markets conventional capital may overlook. And practitioners, funders, researchers and policymakers are meeting in Nairobi through Wayfinder to discuss what the next phase of social innovation should look like.

For African founders, the practical discipline is straightforward but demanding. Be clear about who experiences the value and who pays. Measure evidence that can change an actual decision. Match the financing instrument to the economics of the enterprise instead of treating every capital need as a grant problem. And design growth so that the mission, quality and economics survive expansion.

Impact should not be a reporting layer added after the business model. Where possible, it should be connected to the value proposition itself—and where the outcome is a public good, the enterprise should be explicit about the complementary public, philanthropic or blended financing still required.
